item.title: Germany men's soccer team wears home brand Adidas one last time before Nike takes over
item.description: Germany’s men’s soccer team was wearing Adidas gear for the last time on Monday as their association of more than 70 years was ending.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: BERLIN — Germany’s men’s soccer team was wearing Adidas gear for the last time on Monday as their association of more than 70 years was ending. American sportswear giant Nike is poised to take over next year. Germany defeated the Netherlands 5-0 in Berlin’s Olympiastadion in their Nations League showdown to be sure of reaching the quarterfinals. Germany coach Jürgen Klopp wore his usual Adidas cap with the German colours and the slogan “One of 83 million” referencing the country’s population. He’ll likely be forced to find another cap for his next game in charge. Nike’s takeover caught many by surprise when it was announced in March 2024, with the German soccer federation (DFB) forced to defend the deal running to 2034 from criticism – ultimately it came down to money. “Nike made by far the best financial offer in the transparent and non-discriminatory tender process,” the DFB said at the time. It ended an association going back to the 1954 World Cup when Adi Dassler — the founder of the German sportswear brand with echoes of his name — sat on the bench beside West Germany coach Sepp Herberger. The Germans won the trophy for the first time with Dassler’s company’s screw-in stud boots. Dassler did not invent the boots with changeable studs, as many believe. German shoemaker Alexander Salot came up with that idea and registered his invention with the German patent office on Aug. 30, 1949. But they did help West Germany beat Hungary in the 1954 World Cup final. Dassler’s company went on to supply German soccer with its gear ever since. It was worn when West Germany and then the reunified country won another three men’s World Cup titles (1974, 1990, 2014). Germany’s women’s team also wore Adidas gear as it won two World Cup titles in 2003 and 2007.

item.title: Nvidia rules out Jensen Huang comeback as campaign for his return grows
item.description: Nvidia’s board is not weighing a return for Jensen Huang as CEO, sources told Reuters, days after affairs forced his resignation.
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: WASHINGTON — Nvidia’s board is not weighing a return for Jensen Huang as CEO, three people told Reuters, despite a growing campaign for his return days after affairs involving employees and suspected Chinese intelligence ties forced his resignation. More than 180,200 people have signed a petition demanding Huang’s return, Elon Musk has thrown his support behind the effort, and U.S. President Donald Trump said he would not mind seeing Huang reinstated as CEO. Thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees have joined the call, even as governance experts and some investors warn that bringing him back before investigations are complete could expose the company to fresh risks. The groundswell of support for Huang has turned a corporate succession story into a test of whether Nvidia can separate itself from a founder whose influence stretches across its employees — some fiercely loyal to the former CEO — and shareholders, Silicon Valley, the Taiwanese supply chain and Washington. Taiwan’s tallest skyscraper, Taipei 101, was illuminated on Monday with messages including “Taiwan Loves Jensen.” Some prominent shareholders such as Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker and Altimeter Capital Management CEO Brad Gerstner have urged Nvidia not to rush to replace him before all the facts are known. “The Nvidia board is not considering bringing Jensen back,” one of the people familiar with the matter said. The support for the former CEO, who acknowledged having an affair with a Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, comes as U.S. intelligence agencies are still trying to determine the extent of her relationship with China’s Ministry of State Security and what information she may have passed to Beijing, according to two sources familiar with the matter. Evidence gathered so far indicates she was likely an intelligence asset, someone who shared information, rather than a fully trained spy, the sources said. The uncertainty has divided investors over Huang’s future and complicated the board’s search for a successor. Nvidia shares closed down more than four per cent on Monday, a day before the chipmaker is due to report third-quarter earnings. Since news of Huang’s intimate relationship broke, Nvidia has lost US$800 billion in market value and the stock’s price-to-earnings ratio has dropped to 11.54 from 15.59, well below the 20.8 average for the Nasdaq Composite. Big names back Huang The “Stand With Jensen” campaign listed SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney among its signatories. The campaign website showed more than 8,800 signatories identified themselves as current Nvidia employees and more than 94,000 as shareholders, though it cautioned that professional affiliations were self-reported and had not been independently verified. “We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the Board: bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts,” an open letter on the website said. Huang stepped down on Thursday after reports of alleged affairs with employees, including one who reported directly to him, plunging the AI chip heavyweight into crisis and sending shockwaves through an industry he helped bankroll. “I think he learned a big lesson,” Trump said on Monday. Trump’s reported trades this year suggest he held between US$13 million and US$62 million in Nvidia stock as of the end of August, the Washington Post reported on Monday, citing a review of his financial disclosures. The Trump administration said on Monday it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips, tightening controls as President Donald Trump headed to China for talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Large investors are risk averse Large investors may prove harder to persuade about reinstating Huang. One institutional investor in Nvidia stock, speaking on condition of anonymity, said they would be wary of Huang returning to Nvidia, adding that other big companies, including Apple and Microsoft, had thrived after their visionary CEOs had left. Richard Windsor, an independent technology researcher, said he expected large institutional Nvidia investors to oppose Huang’s return while investigations remained unresolved because of the legal exposure and uncertainty it could create. “They’re very risk-averse,” Windsor said, but he added that his own view was that Nvidia shareholders would ultimately be better served by Huang’s return because of the relationships he has built with the company’s customers and suppliers. T Rowe Price analysts said in a note that a transition of power may call for a new organizational structure rather than simply a new executive. Huang’s exit rocks Taiwan Huang’s reach is especially visible in Taiwan, where he was born, and where he enjoys celebrity-like status dubbed “Jensanity.” Nvidia relies on TSMC, which manufactures Nvidia’s most advanced chips, and a sprawling network of suppliers to manufacture the chips and systems underpinning the AI boom. For many Taiwanese, Huang’s exit marks the loss of a charismatic champion who helped put the island at the heart of the global artificial intelligence boom, with his influence extending well beyond the technology industry. Jimmy Yang, 42, who works in marketing, said Huang’s departure was a loss for Taiwan, where his influence had extended to local businesses and tourism, and Yang expressed hope that Huang could eventually return to Nvidia. “His private life is his own choice,” Yang said. “But whether it’s the night market economy he’s driven or his help for the tech industry, it has been massive.” (Reporting by Ross Kerber, Alexandra Alper, Karen Freifeld and Jeffrey Dastin; Additional reporting by Jaspreet Singh, Wen-Yee Lee, Fabian Hamacher and Erin Banco; Writing by Sayantani Ghosh; Editing by Christian Plumb, Anil D’Silva, Nick Zieminski and Daniel Wallis) Ross Kerber, Alexandra Alper, Jeffrey Dastin and Karen Freifeld, Reuters

item.title: Tiff Macklem to step down as Bank of Canada governor at end of his term
item.description: The Bank of Canada says Tiff Macklem will not seek a second term as governor and plans to step down when his current run expires on June 2, 2027.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA — Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem will step down at the end of his term, which began in the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic and saw him navigating the central bank through the subsequent period of higher inflation.   “It has been the highlight of my career to serve as the 10th governor of the Bank of Canada,” Macklem said in a news release Monday. He said his tenure came as Canada navigates a world that is more fragmented and shock-prone. “The bank has faced these challenges by acting decisively, by using sound judgment in the face of uncertainty, and by serving Canadians with humility and a steadfast commitment to its mandate,” he said.  Macklem was named governor in May 2020 and took over the top job in June of that year, overseeing the bulk of Canada’s monetary policy response to the COVID-19 pandemic.  At the time of the appointment, he was the dean of the business school at the University of Toronto. Macklem was also a former second-in-command at the Bank of Canada, serving as senior deputy governor between 2010 and 2014 when Prime Minister Mark Carney headed the Bank of Canada. In March 2020, a few months before Macklem took over, the Bank of Canada cut interest rates to the emergency level of 0.25 per cent in an effort to help the economy weather the shock.  Two years later, the central bank began a historic interest rate hiking campaign to bring inflation down to its two per cent target level. Canadians should be thankful for Macklem’s service, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said Monday while speaking to reporters on Monday.  “He’s been doing a good service to Canadians and serving for a long time ... there’s a normal course of things that you would launch a selection process to replace him in due course,” he said. “But today is the moment to say thank you governor for your service to the nation, your service to Canadians and the Canadian economy.” The central bank’s board of directors says it has started a search process to select the next governor, with the recruitment process expected to be completed by the spring.  The next governor is slated to serve a seven-year term beginning June 3, 2027.  The board’s choice will be subject to approval by the minister of finance and the federal cabinet. Potential successors to Macklem include Bank of Canada senior deputy governor Carolyn Rogers. She serves as the bank’s second-in-command, however, the person holding that position has been passed over for the top job in recent decades. Carolyn Wilkins, who served as senior deputy governor from May 2014 to December 2020, is also a potential candidate after playing a key role in the central bank’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic. Likely private sector candidates include Jean Boivin, the head of BlackRock Investment Institute, and Scotiabank chief economist Jean-François Perrault. Both Boivin and Perrault have previously held positions at the central bank and in government. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

item.title: Higher gas, grocery prices keep inflation elevated at 3.1% despite relief elsewhere
item.description: Canada’s inflation rate held steady in October as higher prices for gas, groceries and clothes were partly offset by cheaper cellphone plans and slower rent price growth, Statistics Canada said Monday ...
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA -- Canada’s inflation rate held steady in October as higher prices for gas, groceries and clothes were partly offset by cheaper cellphone plans and slower rent price growth, Statistics Canada said Monday. The annual rate of inflation was steady at 3.1 per cent last month, slightly below economists’ expectations of 3.2 per cent. The inflation reading raises questions about whether the Bank of Canada will need to raise interest rates again in December, said Benjamin Reitzes, BMO’s managing director of Canadian rates and macro strategist. “There’s nothing in these numbers at the moment that really screams rate hike for the Bank of Canada,” he said. “They’ve been particularly hawkish over the past few weeks and they raised rates in October and signalled that more could be necessary.” Reitzes said October’s inflation numbers “don’t necessarily signal that they need to do something immediately, but again, that doesn’t mean they won’t. There’s no clearcut case here either way.” Gasoline continued to be a key driver of headline inflation, rising 30.9 per cent year-over-year in October compared with 27.8 per cent the month before amid continued conflict in the Middle East and Ukraine. Higher energy costs could eventually push up prices elsewhere, said Royal Bank of Canada economist Abbey Xu. “The longer energy prices remain elevated, the more cost pressures will filter through to consumer prices with a lag,” she said in a client note.  “The path of energy prices also remains highly uncertain despite the decline in gasoline prices so far in November.” StatCan said gasoline prices rose at a faster annual pace last month partly because prices fell sharply in October 2025, making the year-over-year increase appear larger. On a monthly basis, however, gasoline prices fell 2.5 per cent in October. Excluding energy, annual inflation eased to two per cent in October from 2.1 per cent in September. “Underlying price pressures stayed comparatively contained,” Xu said, noting that the consumer price index excluding both food and energy slowed to 1.8 per cent.  RBC’s diffusion index, which measures how widespread inflation is across the economy, continued to show that “unusually strong price growth has been concentrated in a relatively narrow share of the consumer basket,” she said.  Meanwhile, Canadians once again faced higher prices at grocery stores. StatCan said the cost of food purchased from stores accelerated to two per cent year-over-year in October after four consecutive months of slower price growth. Fresh vegetable prices rose 1.4 per cent year-over-year in October after falling 2.9 per cent in September while condiments, spices and vinegars were up 2.6 per cent. Compared with October 2020, the agency said grocery prices have climbed 31.9 per cent. Even as inflation slows, Canadians are still feeling the effects of years of rising prices, Reitzes said. “The reality is inflation is only prices going higher; prices don’t come back down in general,” he said. “What we need to happen is a lengthy period of relatively low inflation and some good wage growth and that’ll make everyday Canadians feel much better.” Meanwhile, prices for clothing were up 1.8 per cent in October, driven by a 2.2 per cent year-over-year increase in women’s clothing and a 1.4 per cent increase in men’s clothing. Clothing prices were up 3.4 per cent month-over-month in October, the largest monthly increase since September 2019. StatCan said the price increases coincided with higher shipping costs. In Ontario, prices for natural gas rose three per cent year-over-year in October after declining 18.7 per cent in September. Prices for cellphone plans fell 6.2 per cent year-over-year in October, after rising 0.8 per cent in September. StatCan said the decline was largely due to comparisons with a year ago, when companies had raised prices. Slower rent price growth also helped ease inflation, particularly in British Columbia, while rents in Ontario rose 1.1 per cent year-over-year in October. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026. By Brett Bundale
